Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 54, verses 1–8:

(p-136) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surat al-Qamar

It is a Meccan surah by consensus, except for one verse about which there is disagreement. The majority of people said: it is Meccan. A group said: it was revealed on the day of Badr. It was also said: it was revealed in Medina, and this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45]. The discussion of this will come later.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split.﴾ ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "This is continuous magic."﴾ ﴿And they denied and followed their desires, and every matter is settled.﴾ ﴿And there has certainly come to them of the news that which contains a deterrent.﴾ ﴿Far-reaching wisdom, but warnings avail not.﴾ ﴿So turn away from them. The Day the caller calls to a terrible thing.﴾ ﴿Their eyes humbled, they will emerge from the graves as if they were scattered locusts.﴾ ﴿Hastening toward the caller. The disbelievers will say, "This is a difficult day."﴾

"Iqtarabat" means: it drew near, but it is more emphatic, just as iqtadara is more emphatic than qadara. "As-sa'ah" (the Hour) is the Resurrection, and its timing is unknown; it is not known except that it has drawn near, without a specific determination. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I and the Hour have been sent like these two," and he pointed with the index and middle fingers. Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ delivered a sermon when the sun was almost setting, and he said: 'What remains of the world compared to what has passed is only like what remains of this day compared to what has passed.'" The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also said: "I truly hope that Allah will delay my community by half a day." This was from him ﷺ by way of hope and supposition, not a definite report. So Allah, exalted is He, fulfilled his hope and delayed his community more than he hoped. Whatever is narrated about determining the age of the world is weak and feeble.

His saying, exalted is He: "the moon has split" is a report of what occurred in that event. Ath-Tha'labi mentioned concerning this that it was said: the meaning is "the moon will split on that day," but this is weak and the community is against it. That is because the Quraysh asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a sign, and it was said: it was general, and this is the view of the majority. It was also said: rather, they specified the splitting of the moon, which ath-Tha'labi mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. "So Allah, exalted is He, showed them the splitting of the moon, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and a group of Muslims and disbelievers saw it, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Bear witness.'" Among the Companions who said "I saw it" were 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Jubayr ibn Mut'im, (p-138) and he informed 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, Anas, Ibn 'Abbas, and Huthayfah ibn al-Yaman [of it]. The polytheists said at that: "Muhammad has bewitched us," and some of them said: "He has bewitched the moon." The Quraysh said: "Ask the travelers who arrive among you," and no one came except that he informed of its splitting. Ibn Mas'ud said: "I saw it split, and a group went behind Mount Hira'." Ibn Zayd said: "One half of it was seen over Qu'aiqi'an and the other over Abu Qubays." Huthayfah recited: "The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has [already] split," and ath-Tha'labi mentioned from him that his recitation was: "The Hour has drawn near, the moon split," without a waw.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away﴾ — the wording came in the present tense so as to encompass what has passed and what will come; it is a report that their state is thus. People differed regarding the meaning of "mustamirr" (continuous). Az-Zajjaj said: it has been said that its meaning is lasting and persistent. Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Kisa'i, and al-Farra' said: its meaning is passing away, going by, soon to vanish. Ad-Dahhak and Abu al-'Aliyah said: its meaning is tightly bound with strands of rope, as if the magic had been made firm (istamarra), i.e., made strong. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Until its firmness was established upon a rock, the true resolve, neither weak nor feeble."

Then Allah, exalted is He, reported that they denied and followed their desires and what they wished of matters, without evidence and without verification. Then He said, exalted is He, in the form of a definite report: ﴿and every matter is settled﴾, as if He, exalted is He, were saying: every thing has an end. The truth will be settled, established and manifest, and falsehood will be settled, vanished and gone. (p-139) Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read: "wa kullu amrin mustaqirrin" with a genitive on "mustaqirrin", meaning by it its portents. The majority read the qaf of "mustaqirr" with a kasra. Nafi' — with a variant — and Ibn Nisah read it with a fatha. Abu Hatim said: there is no basis for the fatha.

"Al-anba'" is the plural of naba', and this encompasses everything the Qur'an brings of admonitions, stories, and examples of disbelieving nations. "Muzdajar" means: a place of deterrence and cessation. Its origin is "muztajar"; the taa' was changed to a daal to make its articulation point closer to that of the zay, and similarly the taa' of ifta'ala is changed from every verb whose first letter is a zay, such as izdalafa, izdad, and the like.

His saying, exalted is He: "hikmah" (wisdom) is in the nominative, either as an apposition to "ma" in His saying "ma fihi," or as the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being: this is wisdom. "Baligha" (far-reaching) means: it reaches its aim through admonishing souls and making clear to whoever has intellect. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿but warnings avail not﴾ — "ma" may be negating, i.e., the warnings do not avail with the obstinacy of these people; or it may be interrogative in the sense of affirmation, i.e., what is the benefit of warnings with these disbelievers?

Then Allah, exalted is He, consoled His Prophet, peace be upon him, with His saying: "So turn away from them," i.e., do not let your soul go out in sorrow over them. The statement is complete at His saying "from them," and then their threat begins. The governing element of "yawma" (the Day) is His saying "yakhrujun" (they will emerge). "Khushsha'an" is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in "yakhrujun," and the conjugation of the verb requires the circumstance to precede. Al-Mahdawi said: it may also be a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in "'anhum." Al-Rummani said: the meaning is: so turn away from them and remember the Day. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is: so turn away from them today. The waw was dropped from "yad'u" because the scribes of the Mushaf followed the pronunciation, not what orthography requires. As for dropping the yaa' from "al-da'i" and the like, Sibawayh said: they dropped it for lightness. Abu 'Ali said: it was dropped together with the alif and lam, since it is dropped along with what replaces them, which is tanwin.

The majority of reciters read "ila shay'in nukur" with a damma on the kaf. Ibn Kathir, Shibl, and al-Hasan read "nukr" with a sukun on the kaf. Mujahid, al-Jahdari, and Abu Qilabah read "nukira" with a kasra on the kaf and a fatha on the ra', as a passive. The meaning in all of this is that it is unfamiliar, not recognized, and its like is not seen. Al-Khalil said: "nukr" is an adjective for a severe matter and a clever man. Malik ibn 'Awf al-Nadri said: (p-140)

"Advance, Muhaj, for it is a day of nukr, my like against your like, defending and charging."

"Nukr" is of the form fu'ul, and it is an adjective, which is rare among adjectives; from it is "mishyatun sujuh" (a gentle gait). The poet said:

"Leave off the swaggering and walk with a gentle gait, for men are of might and remembrance."

Similar to it are "rajulun shalul" and "naqatun ujud."

The majority of reciters read "khushsha'an," which is the reading of al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-Hasan, and Qatadah. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "khashi'an," which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Jahdari; it is singular with the meaning of plural, and its parallel is the poet's saying:

"And youths whose faces are handsome, from Iyad ibn Nizar ibn Ma'add."

(p-141) Abu Hatim preferred this reading, and he mentioned that a man from among the volunteers said before he was martyred: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream and asked him about 'khushsha'an' and 'khashi'an,' and he said: 'khashi'an,' with an alif." It is also in the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both, as "khashi'an." Allah, exalted is He, singled out the eyes for humility because it is more apparent in them than in the rest of the limbs; likewise, everything in a person's soul, whether shame, arrogance, fear, or the like, becomes apparent only in the gaze.

"Al-ajdath" is the plural of jadath, which is the grave. He likened them to scattered locust, and in another place He likened them to scattered moths, and they have a resemblance to both. Some exegetes held that at first they are like moths when they surge among one another, and then at another stage like locusts when they head toward the place of assembly and the caller. In a hadith: "Maryam bint 'Imran, peace be upon her, invoked against the locusts, saying: 'O Allah, cause them to perish without suckling, and let their sons follow without spreading.'"

"Al-muhti'": one who hastens in his walk toward a thing, with a shaking and a running, and extending the gaze toward the destination, whether out of fear, hope, or the like. ﴿The disbelievers will say, "This is a difficult day,"﴾ because of what they see of the signs of its terror and the marks of its hardship.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿The people of Noah denied before them; they denied Our servant and said, "Mad!" and he was rebuked.﴾ ﴿So he called upon his Lord: "I am overpowered, so give victory."﴾ ﴿So We opened the gates of the heaven with water pouring forth.﴾ ﴿And We caused the earth to burst forth with springs, so the waters met for a matter that had been decreed.﴾ ﴿And We carried him on [a vessel] of planks and nails.﴾ ﴿Running under Our eyes, as a recompense for one who had been denied.﴾ ﴿And We have left it as a sign, so is there any who will remember?﴾ ﴿So how was My punishment and warning?﴾ ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾

The recounting of this story is a threat to Quraysh and a parable for them. His saying, the Exalted, "wazdujir" (and he was rebuked), is information from Allah the Exalted that they rebuked Noah, peace be upon him, with abuse, threats and intimidation. This was said by Ibn Zayd, who recited: ﴿If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 116]. Mujahid held that "wazdujir" (and he was rebuked) is part of the speech of Noah's people, as if they said, "Mad, and rebuked," meaning: he has been driven to madness and inflamed with madness. This is a view containing forced interpretation and arbitrariness.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, al-A'raj and al-Hasan read "anni" (that I) with a fatha on the alif, i.e. "bi-anni" (that I), as if his supplication had this meaning. **Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah 54, verses 18–26:**

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿'Ad denied, so how was My punishment and My warnings!﴾ ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind on a day of continuous misfortune,﴾ ﴿plucking people up as if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees.﴾ ﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings!﴾ ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ ﴿Thamud denied the warnings,﴾ ﴿and they said, "Shall we follow a single human being from among us? Indeed, we would then be in error and madness."﴾ ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him from among us? Rather, he is a liar and an insolent one.﴾ ﴿They will know tomorrow who the liar and the insolent one is.﴾

"'Ad" is a tribe, and their story has already been mentioned.

As for His saying, ﴿So how was My punishment and My warnings!﴾, the position of "kayfa" (how) is in the accusative. It is either the predicate of "kāna" (was) or a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). In this case, "kāna" means "found" and "occurred." "Nudhur" is the plural of "nadhīr" (warner), which is also the verbal noun (maṣdar). Warsh alone recited "nudhurī" with a ya' (the first-person suffix), and the rest recited "nudhur" without a ya', following the written form of the Muṣḥaf.

As for "ṣarṣar," Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said its meaning is "cold," and it derives from "ṣirr" (cold). A group of exegetes said its meaning is "making a sound," like these two letters, derived from "ṣarrati al-rīḥu" when the wind blows forcefully, as if it is pronouncing these two letters: ṣād and rā'. The verb was doubled, as they say "kabkaba" and "kafkafa" from "kabba" and "kaffa," and this is common. The reciters did not differ on the sukūn (silence) of the ḥā' in "naḥs" and on the idafa (construct phrase) of "yawm" to it, except what is narrated from al-Ḥasan, that he recited "fī yawmin" with tanwīn (nunation) and "naḥisin" with a kasra on the ḥā'. "Mustamirr" means "consecutive." Qatada said: that misfortune continued for them until it brought them to Hell. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said, in al-Tha'labī's book: the meaning is that it was bitter for them. al-Naqqāsh also mentioned this from al-Ḥasan.

It is narrated that the day on which they had continuous misfortune was a Wednesday. Some of the hadiths regarding the interpretation of this verse mention "a day of continuous misfortune, the day of Wednesday." **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 54, verses 36–44:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And Lot had certainly warned them of Our assault, but they disputed the warnings.﴾ ﴿And they had certainly sought to make him surrender his guests, so We obliterated their eyes: "Taste My punishment and warnings."﴾ ﴿And a settled punishment came upon them early in the morning.﴾ ﴿"Taste My punishment and warnings."﴾ ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance; so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ ﴿And the warnings certainly came to the family of Pharaoh.﴾ ﴿They denied all Our signs, so We seized them with the seizure of the Mighty, the Omnipotent.﴾ ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those? Or do you have immunity in the scriptures?﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "We are a united victorious company"?﴾

The meaning: Lot warned his people, and We seized them and struck them, meaning Our punishment for them. "Tamaraw" (they disputed) means they doubted, and some of them passed doubt on to others by engaging in confusions and misguidance. "Al-nudhur" is the plural of nadhir (warner), and it is the verbal noun (masdar). It is possible that by "al-nudhur" here, and in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The people of Lot denied the warnings﴾ [al-Qamar: 33], is meant the plural of nadhir, which is the active participle. "Al-day'" (guests) applies to the singular and the plural, and their guests and their stories have already been mentioned in full.

As for His saying, exalted is He, "So We obliterated their eyes": Qatadah said it is literal: Jibril, peace be upon him, drew some of his wing over their eyes, so they became level with their faces. Abu 'Ubayda said: "obliterated" with skin like the face. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said it is a metaphor (isti'ara), and that He only blocked their perception, so they entered the house and saw nothing, and He made that like obliteration.

As for His saying, exalted is He, "bukra" (early in the morning): it was said that this occurred at sunrise. Ibn Muhaysin assimilated the dal into the sad in His saying, glorified is He: "wa-laqad sabbahahum" (sabbahahum), while the majority read without this assimilation (idghaam). "Bukra" is indefinite here, and for that reason it is declined (ṣurifat).

As for His saying, exalted is He, "Taste My punishment": it may be from God's saying to them, and it may be from the angels' saying. "Nudhur" is the plural of the verbal noun, meaning: and the consequence of My warnings which you denied. He, exalted is He, said "mustaqirr" (settled) describing the punishment, because no reliever removed it from them, but it continued until their death. During the period of their death beneath the earth they are punished, awaiting Hell; then this joins with the punishment of the Fire. So it is a continuous and settled matter. He repeated His saying, exalted is He, "Taste My punishment and warnings" for emphasis and rebuke. Warsh related from Nafi': "wa-nudhurī" with a ya.

"Al i-Fir'awn" (the family of Pharaoh) means his people and followers. From this is the poet's saying:

﴿So do not weep for one dead after another dead, whom 'Ali and 'Abbas and the family of Abu Bakr buried.﴾

He means the Muslims in the burial of the Prophet, peace be upon him. It is possible that by "the family of Pharaoh" is meant his kin, according to the usage of "al" (family), and He singled them out for mention because they were the pillars and the elders of the people.

As for His saying, exalted is He, "They denied Our signs": it is possible that He means the aforementioned family of Pharaoh, whom We seized in this manner, referring to them by the pronoun, because that drowning which occurred in the sea was by might and power. And His saying "Our signs" means by them the nine signs. Then He emphasized it with "all of them." It is possible that His saying, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿And the warnings certainly came to the family of Pharaoh﴾ is a complete statement, and then His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They denied all Our signs﴾ has the pronoun in "they denied" referring to all the nations mentioned, and "all the signs" comes out correctly. His saying, exalted is He, "So We seized them" similarly refers to all the nations mentioned.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those?﴾ and the verse...: it is addressed to the Quraysh, placing them before the matter in the manner of rebuke: Is there a quality of wealth, or strength of bodies and expansiveness, or intellect, or other than that, which requires that you are better than these punished ones who denied? So is salvation from punishment hoped for you, through that excellence, when you denied your Messenger? Or do you have, in the scriptures of God, the sent-down books, immunity from punishment? This was said by al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, and 'Ikrima.

Then God, exalted is He, said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Or do they say that they are a united body, confident that We will be victorious by Our strength, in a manner of self-admiration and arrogance? They will be defeated, so their multitude will not benefit them. Abu Haywa read "am taqulun" (or do you say) with the ta' from above.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "obliterated" with skin like the face. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said it is a metaphor (isti'ara), and that He only blocked their perception, so they entered the house and saw nothing, and He made that like obliteration.

He repeated His saying, exalted is He, "Taste My punishment and warnings" for emphasis and rebuke. Warsh related from Nafi': "wa-nudhurī" with a ya.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 54, verse 45–55:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿Soon will the multitude be routed, and they will turn their backs.﴾ ﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness.﴾ ﴿The Day they are dragged into the Fire upon their faces: "Taste the touch of Saqar!"﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure.﴾ ﴿And Our command is but one word, like a glance of the eye.﴾ ﴿And We have already destroyed your like, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ ﴿And everything they have done is in the scriptures.﴾ ﴿And every small and great matter is recorded.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and rivers.﴾ ﴿In a seat of truth, in the presence of a Sovereign, Omnipotent.﴾

This is a promise from Allah the Exalted to His Messenger ﷺ that the multitude of Quraysh will be routed, as a victory for him. The majority hold that the verse is Meccan, and it is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I used to say to myself: 'Which multitude will be routed?' When the Day of Badr came, I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in his armour, and he was saying: ﴿Soon will the multitude be routed, and they will turn their backs.﴾"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Indeed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at Badr was citing the verse as evidence.

Some people said: the verse was revealed on the Day of Badr, but that is weak, and the correct view is that the promise was fulfilled on the Day of Badr. Abu Hatim said: Some reciters read "sayuhzamu" with a fatḥa on the yā' and a kasra on the zāy, with "al-jam'u" in the accusative. (p-154) Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: Abu Haywa read "sanahzimu" with a nūn and a kasra on the zāy, with "al-jam'a" in the accusative, and "watawallūna" with a tā' above.

Then these opinions were set aside, and he turned away from them, being concerned with the matter of the Hour, whose punishment is more severe for them than any defeat or killing. So He said: ﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter.﴾ "Adhā" is the superlative of "dāhiya," which is the great calamity that befalls a person, and "amarru" is from "marārah" (bitterness). The word here is used metaphorically, since it is not something tasted.

Then Allah informed about the criminals that in this world they are in confusion, ruin and loss of guidance, and in the Hereafter they are in burning and kindling, from the place to which they are heading. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the meaning is: in loss and madness, and "su'ur" means madness. Most of the exegetes hold that by "the criminals" here are meant the disbelievers. Some people said: what is meant by the criminals is the Qadariyya, who say that the actions of servants are not by the decree of Allah the Exalted.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They are those threatened with being dragged in Hell. Sahb means dragging. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "ila al-nar" (into the Fire).

His saying the Exalted: "fadhuqū" is a metaphor, and the meaning is: it will be said to them, "Taste," by way of rebuke.

People differed concerning His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything according to a measure.﴾ The majority of people read "innā kulla shay'in" with the accusative, and they said: the meaning is: Indeed We created everything, "khalaqnāhu" [We created it] by a measure. "Khalaqnāhu" is not in the position of a qualifier to "shay'in," rather it is a verb indicating a hidden verb. This meaning implies that everything is created, except what the rational proof establishes is not created, such as the Qur'an and the attributes. Abu al-Sammal read — and Abu al-Fath preferred it — "innā kullu" with the nominative, as the subject, with "khalaqnāhu bi-qadarin" as the predicate. Abu Hatim said: "This is the correct form in Arabic, but our reading is with the accusative, along with the majority."

(p-155) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some of the People of the Sunna read it with the nominative, and their meaning is, in the manner of what the earlier ones held, that everything is created with a prior decree. "Khalaqnāhu," on this reading, is not a qualifier to "shay'in." This is the position of the People of the Sunna, and they have a strong argument from the verse for these two views.

The Qadariyya, who say there is no decree and that a person alone is the doer of his actions, read: "innā kullu shay'in khalaqnāhu" with the nominative "kullu," and "khalaqnāhu" is in the position of a qualifier to "kullu," meaning: Indeed Our affair and matter is that everything We created is by a measure, i.e., by a quantity, and according to its form, its time and other than that. Thus by this interpretation they remove the place of the proof against them from the verse.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "I find in the Book of Allah the Exalted people who are dragged in (p-156) the Fire upon their faces, because they used to deny the decree, saying: a person creates his own actions. I do not see them, so I do not know whether it is something that has passed before us or something that remains."

Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Quraysh disputed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the decree, so this verse was revealed." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, then what is the point of action? Is it in something we are beginning, or in something already finished?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Act, for each is made easy for what he was created for. We shall make him easy for ease; We shall make him easy for hardship."

Anas ibn Malik said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The Qadariyya are those who say that good and evil are in our hands. They have no share in my intercession, and I am not of them, nor are they of me."

His saying the Exalted: "illā wāḥidah" means: except one utterance, which is "Be!" His saying the Exalted: "kalamḥin bil-baṣar" is a way of conveying to people the swiftest thing they perceive; and among the matters of Allah the Exalted are things that come about in the blink of an eye. "Al-Ashyā'" are the groups similar in a school of thought and religion and the like; the first is a follower (shī'a) of the second, and the second is a follower of the first.

Then Allah the Exalted informed that every deed of the destroyed nations is written and preserved against them until the Day of Reckoning. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. "Saṭartu" and "asṭartu" have the same meaning. It is narrated from 'Asim that he doubled the rā' in "mustaṭarun." Abu 'Amr said: This occurs only in pause, and it is a well-known dialect.

Most people read "wa-nahar" with a fatḥa on the hā' and the nūn, taking it as a noun of genus, meaning rivers, or as meaning abundance in provision and dwellings. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

Abundance of what my hand possessed, I made its opening into a river, so that the one standing behind it sees what lies beyond it.

(p-157) So his saying "anharta" means: I made its opening like a river. Zuhayr al-Farqabi and al-A'mash read "wa-nuhr" with a ḍammah on the nūn and the hā', taking it as the plural of "nahār" (day), since there is no night in Paradise. This is grammatically acceptable but weak in meaning. It may also be the plural of "nahr." Mujahid, Humayd, Abu al-Sammal and al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan read "nahrin" with a sukūn on the hā', as a singular.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ may mean truth as the opposite of falsehood, i.e., in the seat whose report they affirmed. It may also be from your saying "a true return" (i.e., good), and "a man of truth," i.e., virtuous and possessing fine qualities. Most people read "fī maq'adi" as a noun of genus, and 'Uthman al-Batti read "fī maqā'ida" in the plural. "Al-Malik al-Muqtadir" is Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

The commentary on Surah al-Qamar is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

(p-154) Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: Abu Haywa read "sanahzimu" with a nūn and a kasra on the zāy, with "al-jam'a" in the accusative, and "watawallūna" with a tā' above.

So He said: ﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter.﴾ "Adhā" is the superlative of "dāhiya," which is the great calamity that befalls a person, and "amarru" is from "marārah" (bitterness). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the meaning is: in loss and madness, and "su'ur" means madness. Most of the exegetes hold that by "the criminals" here are meant the disbelievers. Some people said: what is meant by the criminals is the Qadariyya, who say that the actions of servants are not by the decree of Allah the Exalted.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

They are those threatened with being dragged in Hell. Sahb means dragging. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "ila al-nar" (into the Fire).

His saying the Exalted: "fadhuqū" is a metaphor, and the meaning is: it will be said to them, "Taste," by way of rebuke.

This meaning implies that everything is created, except what the rational proof establishes is not created, such as the Qur'an and the attributes. Abu al-Sammal read — and Abu al-Fath preferred it — "innā kullu" with the nominative, as the subject, with "khalaqnāhu bi-qadarin" as the predicate. Abu Hatim said: "This is the correct form in Arabic, but our reading is with the accusative, along with the majority."

Thus by this interpretation they remove the place of the proof against them from the verse.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "I find in the Book of Allah the Exalted people who are dragged in (p-156) the Fire upon their faces, because they used to deny the decree, saying: a person creates his own actions.
